items.titel: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
items.anriss: EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels

absaetze.t: The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.

But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”
Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.

Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.
But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

items.titel: ‘Extremely concerning’: Inside a US Army plan to detonate Iowa lead stores
items.anriss: Army plans to invoke emergency powers to detonate 4 tonnes of lead azide in an Iowa town, despite a court-ordered stay.

absaetze.t: The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in Iowa, defying a federal appeals court’s order suspending its permit to do so.
In a fact sheet this weekend, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said that two controlled explosions were scheduled for around noon (06:00 GMT) on Monday.
That announcement follows statements from the Department of Justice, arguing that Tuesday was the cut-off date to carry out a planned detonation.

Lead azide is a key explosive used in military ammunition. The Iowa stockpile has reportedly grown unstable, and Justice Department lawyers have warned that sub-freezing temperatures could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
“The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” their court filing said.
But critics have questioned the army’s rationale for pushing ahead with the planned detonation, despite the court order to pause it.

“Anyone can claim an emergency at any point and do whatever they want. I don’t think people can or should accept that,” said Thien Chau, a lawyer with the legal group Earthjustice, which represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
Chau told Al Jazeera that not enough has been done to mitigate the risk from the explosions, which are expected to release a cloud of lead into the air.
Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure, and the dense metal can cause birth defects, brain damage and infertility.
“Anyone who hears that the army plans to explode nearly 10,000 pounds [4,500kg] of [this chemical] would recognise that that is not normal,” Chau said.
“That is extraordinary, and that is not something that you just take lightly.”
An 11th-hour legal battle
The impending explosions come after a tense legal battle between the US government and environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council.

The groups have questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13. The EPA authorised the Army to move forward with the explosions, originally scheduled for November 20.
The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).
They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.

The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted a pause on Friday. But in a Saturday court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the Army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.

“The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay,” the Justice Department said in its filing.
But Earthjustice has argued that such a manoeuvre would sidestep the court’s authority.

Government lawyers have “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review”, lawyer Rachel Rintelmann wrote in a Friday filing.
A crisis ‘of the Army’s own making’
The controversy centres on a deteriorating stockpile of explosives stored for more than two decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.
The stockpile contains roughly 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of lead azide across 68 barrels, with lead accounting for approximately 6,900 pounds (about 3.1 tonnes) of its chemical mass.
The explosives had been kept in a mixture of water and ethanol to ensure their stability. But in March, military technicians at the facility discovered that the system was breaking down.
According to a court declaration, an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form.

That recrystallisation puts the lead azide at risk of exploding on its own, as a result of temperature charges or even friction. So many crystals had formed that it was no longer safe to even open the barrels, according to the expert.
But on Sunday, Earthjustice released a statement questioning how this problem was allowed to develop in the first place.
“This emergency is of the Army’s own making,” the statement said. “The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. ”
The US Army has said the barrels are set to be detonated in place at the Iowa facility.

But it claims to have explored other options as well. According to the Army’s environmental assessment, it has previously considered two alternatives: chemically neutralising the explosives, or transporting them to an on-site detonation facility.
It rejected both ideas due to concerns that handling or transporting the explosives could trigger an accidental detonation.
Burying the drums, meanwhile, risked subjecting the shock-sensitive material to jolts that could similarly cause an unintended explosion.
What should residents do before and after the explosions?
But the health risks of even a planned explosion have put residents and environmental groups on edge.
On November 15, the Army released two plume maps outlining the potential spread of lead contamination across a swath of eastern Iowa, though projections hinge on real-time wind conditions.

The first map traces what could happen if a lead-bearing plume drifts northward, with a potential airborne trajectory over communities like Burlington, Muscatine, Davenport, Iowa City and Cedar Rapids.
The second map presents a more tenacious problem: surface exposure.
As the plume tracks north, heavier lead-bearing particles are expected to coat the landscape, landing on outdoor furniture, cars, soil and crops.
Residents in the projected plume path were advised to shelter indoors with their pets, shut windows, and limit exposure to outdoor air during a precautionary period, pending the Army’s all-clear.
Those living near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park were also instructed to leave their homes for six hours to avoid ground vibrations that could crack or shatter nearby windows.
In the plume’s aftermath, the Army said residents would need to hose down outdoor surfaces, vehicles, and play equipment in an effort to flush away any lead dust deposited during the detonation.
But experts have expressed doubt about how practical the safety guidance is.

At a news briefing, University of Iowa professor David Cwiertny, the director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination, warned that long-term monitoring would be necessary to track the lead’s distribution.
“We know that, unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil because those surfaces are hard to clean,” Cwiertny said.

“We will ultimately need to rely on actual field samples after the event to measure how much lead settles there and understand what it means for our land, those crops and the quality of the environment.”
The Army has yet to issue revised instructions or specify new evacuation hours following the delayed detonation.
Earthjustice lawyers like Chau say the lack of communication is part of the problem.
“The way they’ve gone about notifying people and claiming that they’re going to clean things up when they don’t even know the extent of impact, that is extremely concerning,” Chau told Al Jazeera.
Weather concerns?
US Representative Eric Sorensen, the only meteorologist serving in Congress, said the Army should be looking at a window of opportunity that presents the least potential for off-site exposure.
In a video posted on Thursday, Sorensen said, “The most optimum conditions for controlled detonation would be when we have an inversion of clouds, warm air over cool, with light winds.”

He warned that the National Weather Service’s forecast does not offer those favourable conditions over the coming week, and he questioned why the detonations were only announced when cold weather was imminent.
Other questions remain about whether the Army has exhausted every practicable means of containing the lead’s spread.

Bruce Lanphear, a paediatric epidemiologist and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University, told Al Jazeera that it should be up to the Army to provide credible estimates of airborne lead concentrations, ground-level deposition and exposure levels before taking action.
“The burden should be on them to demonstrate that this is the least harmful option, not merely the fastest way to eliminate an immediate danger,” Lanphear told Al Jazeera.

items.titel: Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
items.anriss: Polish confirmation comes after Copenhagen reveals alleged Russian plot to kill US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil.

absaetze.t: Polish confirmation comes after Copenhagen reveals alleged Russian plot to kill US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil.

Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil.
The alleged assassination plan targeted Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and US citizenship, according to Danish media.
Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Maciej Wewior confirmed the alleged plot to kill Vasiliev in Poland to The Associated Press news agency on Sunday.

On Friday, in response to Denmark’s statement about the alleged assassination plan, Poland’s Foreign Ministry had written, “It is the second assassination attempt against the same person. The first one was foiled on the Polish territory in August 2026.”
It also said that a Russian national had been arrested.
Polish authorities detained the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.
Denmark announced the expulsion of a Russian diplomat on Friday after it accused Moscow intelligence of plotting the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September.
Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said on the same day that it suspected Russia of planning the assassination with the help of a banned Danish gang.
Two Danish men appeared ⁠in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder.
Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying they were unsubstantiated.

Previously, on August 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed that a plot to kill a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw was thwarted. He did not disclose Vasiliev’s name at the time but said the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government.
Support for Ukraine
Vasiliev has expressed his support for Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing war on the country and was performing across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.

Russia’s domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defence enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU.
Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations.
Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told reporters on Friday that Denmark was also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians.
Poland’s Foreign Ministry said it backed the move.
“Poland supports measures Denmark suggested to limit the access and freedom of travel of Russian nationals on the EU territory,” it said on X.
Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia has denied those accusations.

items.titel: 99% du territoire de Gaza contaminé par la guerre, selon un rapport d'Oxfam
items.anriss: Plus de 99 % de la bande de Gaza présente des indicateurs de contamination environnementale liée à l'offensive militaire israélienne, nous apprend un rapport publié ce lundi 22 novembre par l’ONG Oxfam et l'Observatoire des conflits et de …

absaetze.t: Plus de 99 % de la bande de Gaza présente des indicateurs de contamination environnementale liée à l'offensive militaire israélienne, nous apprend un rapport publié ce lundi 22 novembre par l’ONG Oxfam et l'Observatoire des conflits et de l'environnement, basé sur des images satellite, la télédétection, et des analyses scientifiques. Résidus d’explosifs, métaux lourds, amiante provenant des bâtiments détruits, eaux souterraines souillées, l'offensive militaire israélienne a créé des risques de contamination généralisés menaçant la santé publique et la survie des habitants de Gaza.
2 min Temps de lecture

Le chiffre est vertigineux. Les opérations militaires israéliennes ont généré plus de 61 millions de tonnes de gravats avec des conséquences terribles. Louis-Nicolas Jandeaux, responsable du plaidoyer chez Oxfam France.

« Dans ces gravats, il y a de l'amiante. C'est aussi des particules qui vont rentrer dans le sol. Évidemment, cela provoque aussi une pollution de l'air absolument terrible. Les poussières issues des bâtiments détruits et de la combustion des déchets provoquent des troubles respiratoires et des lésions pulmonaires terribles pour une part importante de la population gazaouis actuellement. »
Des eaux contaminées aux conséquences mortelles

Chaque jour, d’après le rapport, 40 000 m³ d’eaux usées se déversent dans la mer, une conséquence de la destruction du système d’assainissement. Et 20 % des puits sont contaminés par des matières fécales. « La consommation d'une eau contaminée, l'utilisation d'une eau contaminée pour son hygiène, etc. sont synonymes de maladie. Et c'est aussi synonyme de décès », prévient-il.

Une situation critique qui compromet toute perspective d’avenir. « Aujourd'hui, il y a un enjeu à ce que l'agriculture puisse être relancée, etc. Mais faire pousser sur des sols qui sont contaminés par de l'amiante, par des eaux usées, c'est un danger immense pour la population gazaouis. » Et Louis-Nicolas Jandeaux de prévenir : « La restauration de l'environnement doit être une priorité immédiate et une composante essentielle de la reconstruction de Gaza. »
Une reconstruction rendue impossible par le refus d'Israël d'accorder un accès indépendant à la bande de Gaza.
À écouter aussiQuestions d'environnement – Y a-t-il un écocide à Gaza?

items.titel: US-Repräsentantenhaus: Demokraten so stark wie zuletzt 1992
items.anriss: Die Demokraten haben ihre Mehrheit im US-Repräsentantenhaus weiter ausgebaut. Ab Januar stellen sie dort mindestens 258 Abgeordnete - zuletzt gelang ihnen dies vor mehr als 30 Jahren zu Zeiten von Bill Clinton.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Die Demokraten haben ihre Mehrheit im US-Repräsentantenhaus weiter ausgebaut. Ab Januar stellen sie dort mindestens 258 Abgeordnete - zuletzt gelang ihnen dies vor mehr als 30 Jahren zu Zeiten von Bill Clinton.
Die Demokraten haben bei den US-Kongresswahlen mindestens 258 der 435 Sitze im Repräsentantenhaus gewonnen und damit ihr bestes Ergebnis seit 1992 erzielt.

Die historische Marke wurde am Sonntag erreicht, nachdem der Demokrat Chuck Hubbard im US-Bundesstaat North Carolina die langjährige republikanische Abgeordnete Virginia Foxx besiegt hatte. Nach einer Nachzählung lag Hubbard mit lediglich 330 Stimmen vorn.
Nach der Wahl vom 3. November ist das Rennen um vier Mandate im Repräsentantenhaus noch offen. Die Republikaner kommen bislang auf 173 Sitze.

"Die Demokraten im Repräsentantenhaus haben sich soeben die größte Mehrheit gesichert, die eine Partei im Kongress in diesem Jahrhundert innehatte", erklärte Fraktionschef Hakeem Jeffries, der voraussichtlich Vorsitzender der Kongresskammer wird.
Ab Januar Kontrolle in beiden Kongresskammern

Zuletzt hatten die Demokraten Kongressdaten zufolge im Jahr 1992 genau 258 Sitze gewonnen - es war das Jahr, in dem Bill Clinton zum Präsidenten gewählt wurde. Im Jahr 2008 - das Jahr, in dem Barack Obama die Präsidentenwahl gewann - kamen sie auf 257 Mandate. Die Republikaner hielten ihre stärkste Mehrheit der jüngeren Vergangenheit von 2015 bis 2017 mit 247 Sitzen.

Größere Mehrheiten gab es in früheren Zeiten: In den 1930er Jahren hielten die Demokraten zeitweise 313 oder mehr Sitze. In den 1960er und 1970er Jahren kamen sie vorübergehend auf mehr als 290 Sitze. Die Republikaner erreichten ihre größten Mehrheiten in den 1920er Jahren mit bis zu 302 Mandaten.

Die Demokraten werden ab Januar sowohl das Repräsentantenhaus als auch den Senat kontrollieren. Damit können sie dem republikanischen Präsidenten Donald Trump in der zweiten Hälfte seiner Amtszeit erheblichen Widerstand entgegensetzen. Die deutliche Mehrheit im Repräsentantenhaus verschafft ihnen zudem mehr Spielraum bei parteiinternen Meinungsverschiedenheiten.

items.titel: Ukraine’s Campaign Against Russian Naval Assets Far Beyond The Black Sea Enters A New Phase
items.anriss: A Russian Navy corvette burned and capsized after being struck by Ukrainian uncrewed service vessels (USVs) while docked in Benghazi, Libya. In addition, a Russian cargo ship was struck by Ukrainian USVs while operating off Benghazi in the …

absaetze.t: A Russian Navy corvette burned and capsized after being struck by Ukrainian uncrewed service vessels (USVs) while docked in Benghazi, Libya. In addition, a Russian cargo ship was struck by Ukrainian USVs while operating off Benghazi in the Mediterranean. These strikes follow a suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday. Taken together, they appear to mark a new phase in Kyiv’s campaign to strike at Moscow’s naval capabilities and shipping far beyond the Black Sea.

Satellite images obtained by TWZ show the Project 20380 Steregushchiy class corvette Merkury capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible. Smoke can be seen wafting up, with debris scattered around the dock.
A wider shot shows how far the sea drones had to travel inside the port to hit the Merkury.
An image collected by Planet Labs shows the vessel still in flames before rolling over into the water.
The following image shows the Merkury before it was struck.

The Merkury was docked at the Benghazi port in eastern Libya “when several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya,” The Associated Press reported, citing an initial investigation into the attack. “At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship.”
We cannot confirm if the drones were launched from land, as the AP reports, or a vessel.

Local sources told Al Jazeera late on Sunday the ship “was carrying weapons, ammunition and drones in its cargo. Local sources quoted residents as saying that they saw three drones attack the vessel.”
The ship would have been carrying all these things by default as it is a relatively advanced Russian warship, although it is not typically used for moving cargo.
An “unknown number of Libyan and Russian nationals were killed in the attack at dawn,” the publication added.
Video emerged on social media claiming to show the moment the Merkury was attacked.

Merkury is a very new and modern surface combatant for the Russian Navy. It was commissioned in 2023, the official Ukrainian United24 media outlet reported. “It carries a crew of approximately 90 personnel.”

The Steregushchiy class ships are among Russia’s more modern corvettes. With a standard displacement of 1,800 tons, a length of 343 feet, and a flight deck for a helicopter, the corvettes are closer to frigates, according to some classification systems. Their primary armament consists of two quadruple launchers for Uran anti-ship missiles, a 12-cell Redut vertical launch system for various air defense missiles, and two quadruple tubes for Paket-NK anti-torpedo/anti-submarine torpedoes.

“Although assigned to Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, the warship had been operating from Northern Fleet bases in the Arctic amid the war in Ukraine,” United24 added. A Ukrainian source confirmed to TWZ that the Merkury was struck by sea drones launched by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). The SBU has not commented.
As we noted at the top of this story, the Russian cargo ship Ascalon was also struck by Ukrainian sea drones while off Benghazi.

“According to Ukraine’s military intelligence, Ascalon was used to transport weapons,” the Ukrainian UNN media outlet reported. “The vessel is also considered one of the participants in the so-called ‘Syrian Express’ — a route for supplying military cargo from Russian ports to Syria via the Bosporus.”

“The ship belongs to the Russian company M Leasing LLC, which is under U.S. sanctions for its involvement in transporting military cargo,” UNN added. “Ascalon itself was also placed under U.S. restrictions.”
After the sea drone attacks, Sky News Arabia published an image it said was of one of the vessels that was used.
Video emerged purporting to show the Libyan National Army shooting at one of the sea drones.
These two strikes are a major escalation, but are part of an established pattern of Ukraine hunting for Russian and Russian-affiliated vessels in the Mediterranean going back years.

“These incidents follow a series of attacks and unexplained explosions involving Russian-linked vessels in the Mediterranean, including Ursa Major, Seajewel, Vilamoura and Arctic Metagaz,” the Ambrey maritime security firm told us.
As we reported in December, Ukrainian aerial drones struck a tanker belonging to Russia’s so-called ‘shadow fleet’ in the Mediterranean.

A source from within the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) told TWZ at the time that “a new, unprecedented special operation” was carried out “more than 2,000 kilometers” (1,243 miles) from Ukrainian territory.
The target was the Oman-flagged crude oil tanker Qendil, empty at the time of the attack and sailing from the Indian port of Jamnagar, where it had been unloaded on December 1.

Ukraine’s campaign against Russian naval and shipping assets is growing far beyond the Mediterranean too, with the Baltic Sea, right in Russia’s backyard, quickly becoming a third epicenter beyond the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.
Finnish officials confirmed that a Russian corvette was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Nov. 11, although little is known about the strike, BBC reported at the time.
“Ukraine’s SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia’s Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast,” the publication explained.

In April 2024, there was a fire on a Russian warship at Baltiysk in Kaliningrad. The fire damaged communications and electronic systems aboard the Buyan class corvette Serpukhov. A Ukrainian military intelligence official subsequently claimed that this was the result of a covert joint operation conducted by his GUR agency and a pro-Kyiv Russian military group.
The following video shows the sabotage attack on the Serpukhov.
On June 3, Ukraine struck the Project 20380 Steregushchiy class corvette Boikiy, we reported at the time. That was believed to have been the first strike of its kind against the Baltic Fleet.
The Boikiy is the sister ship of the Merkury, United24 noted.

Then there was the most recent strike. As the Merkury was struck in Benghazi, recovery efforts were underway for the Sparta II, a Russian-owned cargo ship struck by Ukrainian drones on Saturday in the Baltic.
On Sunday, a Russian rescue vessel began towing the Sparta II “out of Finnish waters after two days of firefighting,” Reuters reported, citing Finland’s coast guard.

Commander Ilja Iljin from the Border Guard’s Headquarters “told the Finnish Yle news outlet on Saturday that the Sparta II was hit by Ukrainian drones in Russian territorial waters, lost its steering ability and drifted into Finnish territorial waters. As a result, the responsibility for maritime rescue was transferred to Finland,” the publication reported.

The Ukrainian campaign against Russian shipping “has not been confined to the Black Sea for some time,” Ambrey noted. “Russian naval assets, military logistics and commercial shipping face an expanding threat across the Baltic and Mediterranean.”

As we have frequently noted, many successful Ukrainian USV attacks have been recorded against Black Sea Fleet vessels and facilities, forcing the general evacuation of Russian naval assets from occupied Crimea and to bases in Russia proper. These facilities have all come under attack since the force posture shift.

Though Russia is the target of these sea drone attacks, the incidents highlight vulnerabilities and general uncertainties when it comes to identification of friend or foe for naval drones for all navies, a fact TWZ outlined in detail recently.

Regardless, with three major high-profile strikes, including the destruction of another modern Russian corvette, it is clear that the threat Ukraine poses to Russian shipping and advanced naval assets far from the Black Sea is growing in frequency and magnitude.

items.titel: La Pologne confirme son intérêt pour l’hélicoptère de transport lourd américain CH-47 Chinook
items.anriss: Comme l’a récemment souligné une note du Commandement du combat futur de l’armée de Terre [CFAT], la vulnérabilité d’un hélicoptère de reconnaissance et d’attaque «concerne un ensemble et pas seulement l’appareil dans le ciel» mais aussi …

absaetze.t: Comme l’a récemment souligné une note du Commandement du combat futur de l’armée de Terre [CFAT], la vulnérabilité d’un hélicoptère de reconnaissance et d’attaque «concerne un ensemble et pas seulement l’appareil dans le ciel» mais aussi tout ce qui le fait voler, c’est-à-dire sa chaîne de soutien logistique [maintenance, carburant, etc.].

C’est d’ailleurs pour cette raison que le ministère polonais de la Défense envisage d’acquérir des hélicoptères de transport lourd [HTL] afin d’être en mesure de mettre en place des points de ravitaillement en munitions et en carburant [FARP] pour appuyer les missions des 96 hélicoptères d’attaque AH-64E Apache qu’il a commandés auprès de Boeing. Et cela afin de s’affranchir de toute dépendance à l’égard du transport routier.

«Les Apache auront régulièrement besoin de ravitaillement de maintenance, notamment lors d’opérations intensives et lorsqu’ils opéreront de manière dispersée», a souligné Defence24, le site spécialisé polonais.
En 2024, le ministre polonais de la Défense, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, avait indiqué qu’une réflexion sur l’achat éventuel de tels hélicoptères de transport était en cours.

«Nous avons besoin d’hélicoptères plus gros qui pourraient transporter des charges lourdes et davantage de soldats vers des endroits inaccessibles ou évacuer des personnes», avait en effet déclaré le ministre, avant de laisser entendre qu’un contrat allait être notifié très prochainement. Ce qui n’a pas été le cas.

Quoi qu’il en soit, cette semaine, le vice-ministre polonais de la Défense, Paweł Bejda, a de nouveau évoqué ce sujet en affirmant qu’une partie du prêt de 4 milliards de dollars accordé par les États-Unis à la Pologne au titre de leur Programme de financement militaire étranger [Foreign Military Financing, FMF] pourrait servir à l’achat d’hélicoptères CH-47 Chinook.

Signé en septembre dernier, cet accord de prêt «souligne l’engagement indéfectible des États-Unis envers leur partenariat stratégique avec la Pologne, une relation fondée sur des valeurs partagées de liberté, de prospérité et de respect mutuel», avait justifié la diplomatie américaine.

Et celle-ci d’ajouter : «La Pologne a considérablement renforcé ses capacités de défense ces dernières années, notamment par l’acquisition d’hélicoptères Apache, de systèmes de missiles Patriot, de systèmes HIMARS, de technologies radar avancées et d’avions F-35. Ces investissements consolident la défense nationale polonaise et renforcent la base industrielle de défense américaine».
Reste que, jusqu’à présent, le modèle que le ministère polonais de la Défense envisageait d’acquérir n’avait pas été confirmé.

Outre le CH-47 Chinook, construit par Boeing, Sikorsky, la filiale de Lockheed Martin, propose le CH-53K King Stallion. Autre modèle disponible, européen cette fois : l’AW-101 de l’italien Leonardo, qui en a vendu quatre exemplaires à la marine polonaise.

Cela étant, un choix en faveur du CH-47 Chinook répondrait aux impératifs d’interopérabilité au sein de l’Otan, cet appareil ayant été acquis, entre autres, par les Pays-Bas, l’Allemagne, l’Espagne et le Royaume-Uni.

items.titel: Flooding in southwestern US underlines risks of Trump administration’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument
items.anriss: Recent floods in the Four Corners region of the southwest posed relatively little immediate risk to archaeological sites, but exposed risks due to scaling back of protected areas

absaetze.t: Recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites. The concerns follow the Trump administration’s decision to reduce the monument from more than one million acres to around 120,000 acres, reversing Biden-era protections and dismantling its Indigenous-led management structure.

The decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites. The flooding hit the Four Corners area—which encompasses parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah—from late October to early November, causing widespread damage to roads and infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah says in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable. BLM staff have been patrolling the region to assess road conditions and evaluate the status of infrastructure around areas used for recreation.

“Park rangers and archaeologists have also been assessing cultural sites to identify any potential impacts from the flooding,” the spokesperson says. “While storm events of this nature are not uncommon in this landscape and can affect sensitive cultural resources, no immediate impacts on cultural sites have been reported at this time.”

The local researcher and author Ralph “R.E.” Burrillo was in the town of Bluff, Utah, a gateway to Bears Ears National Monument, when the floods started in late October. He notes that the management plan for the new boundaries has not yet been implemented, so nothing has changed other than the “invisible line”. The longer-term implications, however, remain uncertain.

“With a monument in place, there wouldn’t be these wildcat permits for people supposedly looking to extract resources, but these are just exploratory leases,” he says. “The reality is that there isn’t that much energy to be extracted underground in Bears Ears, or people would have been going after it for decades. When anybody says the monument is locking up America’s energy potential, they are lying.”

Other monuments in the region, like the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, which has substantial deposits of coal and other minerals like uranium, chromium and copper, have a longer history of conflict over resource extraction. The Clinton administration established the monument in 1996 in part to prevent commercial development of coal extraction. Several companies had acquired coal leases in the region during the 1960s and 70s, although commercial mining never materialised.

Burrillo emphasises that the demarcation of the Bears Ears National Monument benefits two constituencies: resource developers and opponents of tribal stewardship. The Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and the Bears Ears National Monument are frequently reduced due to a “handshake deal” that grants energy lobbyists access to energy resources from one site and removes tribal jurisdiction from the latter. At this time, the main immediate threat to heritage sites in the region, Burrillo adds, remains tourism, looting and vandalism.

“What the monument did, at least potentially, was create a nexus for funding to be sent to that area for things like interdiction and law enforcement, education and interpretation, trail maintenance and collaboration with tribes,” Burrillo says. “A monument is a conduit for funding to try to protect those resources from vandals, looters and, again, tourists, who, whether intentionally or not, crawl all over the place. Without the monument, there’s no nexus for funding and that’s really a knock-on effect.”

Although flooding could affect archaeological sites, including potentially eroding petroglyphs, Burrillo says that prehistoric sites in the region are of the least concern. The region has historically flooded, with water sometimes rising to 50ft, and its archaeological sites tell a fascinating story of adaptability, with sites like ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings having been built higher than the water could ever reach. When Mormon pioneers arrived in the region in the 1870s and attempted to establish a town at Bluff, with farms and as an outpost for missioning the Navajo population, they were unsuccessful and eventually moved north.

“When you go back 500 to 2,000 years, the people didn’t have those dams. You simply had this tempestuous river that was famous for flooding more or less constantly, filling miles around the flood basin with water and mud,” Burrillo adds. “The ancestral Pueblo and their ancestors knew it and built above it. For the most part, they treated the river with more respect than we have. The archaeology is in far less danger than the modern infrastructure for that reason.”

items.titel: The tank is back: Ukraine is changing the face of modern warfare once again
items.anriss: Covered in metal rods like hedgehogs, two tanks roar out of cover and race down a country road, escorted by a fleet of flying drones and ground robots. Their prickly armour protects them from enemy drones, allowing them to fire shells into …

absaetze.t: Affairs
November 23, 2026
4 Min Read
Ukrainian forces have reintroduced armoured vehicles to the front lines for the first time in two years, shifting the narrative about the use of redundant tactics in modern warfare.

Covered in metal rods like hedgehogs, two tanks roar out of cover and race down a country road, escorted by a fleet of flying drones and ground robots. Their prickly armour protects them from enemy drones, allowing them to fire shells into trenches and buildings. As the smoke clears, infantry rush forward and capture the positions, while the vehicles race back in the direction that they came from.

This describes footage that was released in October, showing a Ukrainian assault – reportedly using British Challenger 2 tanks – from earlier in the year near the village of Oleksandrivka. Videos from other operations showed Ukraine using a slew of other combat vehicles in a similar fashion, declaring the return of tanks to the Ukrainian front line for the first time in more than two years.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, with Soviet-era T-90s, T-80s and T-72s thundering across the country. Both sides paused military operations over the first winter to rebuild their forces and, by the time Ukraine launched its counteroffensive in June 2023, Russia had built vast defences that could slow down its opponent’s tanks until they were picked off by missiles and artillery. By 2024, drone warfare had made ground combat vehicles so vulnerable that both sides stopped using them.

Military innovation works much like a game of rock, paper, scissors. Force A creates a breakthrough capability (scissors), while force B develops something to counter it (stones), until Force A develops something to overcome that counter (paper).

Tanks were invented by the British during the First World War to cross the Western Front’s killing fields of trenches, barbed wire and machine guns. Armour-piercing weapons and infantry tactics appeared in response. Then tank armour got thicker until the only thing that could take on a tank was another tank. New solutions appeared during the Cold War, such as guided missiles carried by infantry and helicopters. Armoured vehicles, however, have still proven to be battle-winning assets during wars in Israel, Egypt, Iraq, India, Pakistan, Vietnam and the Philippines.

Today, a modern army must carry paper, scissors and stones in what’s called a “combined arms manoeuvre”, where tanks work alongside infantry to defeat enemy soldiers and surface-to-air missiles that knock out aircraft. Modern combat vehicles have new defences too, such as reactive armour.

But the introduction of drones has created a new problem. Unlike other weapons that require the operator to see a tank directly, a drone pilot can be safely out of sight in a bunker many miles away. Drones can also find vehicles hidden far from the front lines and target their top or rear, where the armour is thinner. Their low cost also means that they can be produced en masse, therefore allowing them to overwhelm a tank’s defences: a few drones worth $1,000 (€910) can destroy a tank worth $20m (€18m).

But then came the operation in Oleksandrivska. Ukraine spent months hitting supply lines to starve Russian drone crews of batteries and ammunition. Then it hacked Russian communications to triangulate the country’s positions before targeting them with artillery. The tactic made it possible for Ukrainian tanks to get closer to the combat zone without being spotted, giving them the advantage in retaking territory. If Ukraine can repeat this at a larger scale, the largely static front line of the past few years could start to move.

Despite its drawbacks, nothing beats a tank’s speed, firepower and sturdiness, and militaries are still buying them. Poland will have more than 1,100 by the end of the decade. The next generation of tanks, such as the UK’s Challenger 3 and the US’s M1E3 Abrams, will act as command nodes for drone swarms of their own. It is also those very nations that are training alongside battle-hardened Ukrainians to identify new uses for their inventions. In warfare’s deadly game of rock, paper, scissors, the tank lives on.

items.titel: How can Paris broaden its horizons? By looking beyond its ring-road border
items.anriss: Paris’s banlieues (suburbs) are curious shapeshifters. Once a bucolic, bourgeois retreat away from the dense city, they became the home of factories in the 1830s before descending – unfairly in many cases – into a byword for urban blight. …

absaetze.t: Urbanism
November 23, 2026
3 Min Read

From former factories to old railway infrastructure, Paris’s suburbs are brimming with possibilities for urban development. Here are a few projects that are currently – or should soon be – in the works.

Paris’s banlieues (suburbs) are curious shapeshifters. Once a bucolic, bourgeois retreat away from the dense city, they became the home of factories in the 1830s before descending – unfairly in many cases – into a byword for urban blight.

But several repurposed urban developments suggest that there’s plenty of aspiration to be found beyond the city’s neoclassical boulevards. On the Île Seguin in the western suburb of Boulogne-Billancourt, where Renault’s flagship factory once hummed, contemporary art centre Large opened in October.

This month, a former steel-pipe factory in the northeastern commune of Pantin is gradually reopening with a music hall, bakery and urban-agriculture endeavour. To the northwest, in Clichy-la-Garenne, chef Alain Ducasse will establish a culinary production hub complete with confectionery workshops and a public refectory in mid-December.

By 2027, the Centre Pompidou will inaugurate a giant exhibition space in the southern commune of Massy, proving that Paris’s artistic heft can be redistributed well beyond Baron Haussmann’s Lutetian limestone.
As ambitious initiatives such as these shift perceptions, Parisians are finally seeing the potential of their city’s suburban alter-ego. Here are a few more projects on the capital’s horizon.

Room for manoeuverFirst, the obvious. Building in the suburbs costs up to half as much as in the dense city centre. There are 3,500 hectares of friche (brownfield sites) in the greater Paris region, which is more than in Lisbon or Vienna. And while most of this land is derelict, its industrial past means that there’s old railway infrastructure just waiting to be modernised.

The Grand Paris ExpressThe moniker sounds pompous but the city’s multi-billion-euro Metro expansion is tracking nicely. When Europe’s largest infrastructure project is completed in 2031, its automated (read: strike-proof) trains will zip between Paris’s banlieues and the city’s urban core. It will include 68 new stations dotted along 200km of new tracks, cutting commute times dramatically. The travel time from southern Orly Airport to northern Saint-Denis has halved since line 14’s extension in 2024.

Some clever medallingThe Paris 2024 Summer Olympics also played a role in coaxing Parisians past the maligned périphérique, the orbital road that has come to determine which areas count as part of Paris. The sports event nudged crowds towards the underfunded northern communes, which received 80 per cent of the event’s public investment to build the Athletes’ Village and Aquatic Centre. For two weeks, the city’s centre of gravity shifted and the suburbs became a source of pride rather than a place of perceived penury. The Games weren’t the catalyst for change but they became the deadline. Works that might otherwise have taken 20 years were completed promptly in seven.

Paris’s gritty suburbia is a far cry from the metropolis that postcards betray and tourists crave. But don’t mistake a lack of pearls for a lack of ambition. As France’s capital grows ever more densely populated, and as rents soar, the quieter and less costly suburbs become increasingly appealing. And with another 2.5 billion urban dwellers predicted by 2050, looking to cities’ fringes is a worthwhile place to start. Paris’s resolve for reinvention sends a clear message that, in the peripheries, possibilities abound.

absaetze.t: Le trois-mâts fête ses 130 ans. Le navire, qui a traversé les époques en s’adaptant à différents usages, perpétue aujourd’hui les savoir-faire liés à la navigation sur les grands voiliers et à leur entretien.

Sète, Marseille, Rouen, Bordeaux, Brest, cet été, pour son anniversaire, le Belem s’est offert une tournée des ports français, attirant à chacune des douze étapes de nombreux visiteurs. Un signe de l’intérêt du public pour cette icône du patrimoine maritime tricolore, témoin de 130 ans d’histoire. Pourtant, lorsque le voilier voit le jour, en 1896, aux Chantiers Dubigeon près de Nantes, la grande époque de la marine à voile est déjà presque révolue. Les navires à vapeur ont commencé à concurrencer les voiliers.
Un fleuron de la flotte commerciale au tournant du XXe siècle

Mais le Belem, baptisé ainsi en référence à la cité brésilienne d’où il doit rapporter des fèves de cacao pour le chocolatier Menier, a des arguments. « Il bénéficie des innovations technologiques les plus poussées de cette période », souligne Christelle Hug de Larauze, directrice générale de la Fondation Belem Caisse d’Épargne, propriétaire actuelle du navire.
Doté d’un grand mât d’une hauteur de 34 m et de 22 voiles, le Belem est le dernier des grands voiliers de commerce français du XIXe siècle à naviguer encore aujourd’hui. ©Pierre Bourras.

Outre sa coque en acier riveté, sa capacité de transport de 675 tonnes de cacao, rhum, sucre et autres marchandises, sa barre à roue dotée d’un mécanisme à demi-vis encore utilisée aujourd’hui, il dispose de 22 voiles et d’un gréement en trois-mâts barque. Le mât de misaine, devant, et le grand mât portent des voiles carrées, tandis que le mât d’artimon, à l’arrière, porte un gréement aurique. Des vergues, les pièces horizontales sur lesquelles sont suspendues les voiles carrées, dites « volantes » car capables de coulisser le long du mât améliorent encore sa maniabilité.

Dès son premier voyage, le Belem survit à un incendie. Plus tard, il échappe à l’éruption de la montagne Pelée qui détruit le port de Saint-Pierre en Martinique. Le trois-mâts navigue sous une bonne étoile. Mais c’est aux hommes qui tour à tour l’ont choisi qu’il doit sa longévité exceptionnelle. « À plusieurs reprises, le Belem est repéré, choisi. Il est le bateau élu que ses armateurs successifs, en l’adaptant à leur temps et à de nouveaux usages, ont gardé à la mer, lui permettant de traverser les siècles », note Christelle Hug de Larauzec.
De navire de commerce à yacht de luxe

Ainsi, en 1914, le voilier est racheté par le duc de Westminster, sans doute séduit par son élégance. L’artistocrate britannique transforme le navire de commerce aux 33 campagnes transatlantiques en un yacht de luxe, pour naviguer sur les rives européennes. Doté de moteurs, le navire est agrémenté d’un pont surélevé, de confortables cabines, de différents salons et d’un grand escalier en acajou de Cuba. L’Irlandais Sir Arthur Ernest Guinness, vice-président des brasseries éponymes, poursuit cette transformation après le rachat du Belem, renommé Fantôme II, en 1921. Il fait construire le petit roof, boudoir pour dames devenu aujourd’hui salle à manger des officiers, et équipe le navire pour faire le tour du monde, en famille. Des photos de ses trois filles en robe dans les mâts témoignent de cette période.
Le Grand Roof, un salon d’apparat dont les boiseries ont été restaurées en 2018. ©Dolly.

Désarmé pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, le voilier passe ensuite entre les mains du vicomte italien Vittorio Cini. Rebaptisé Giorgio Cini, du nom du fils perdu de ce nouvel armateur, il est transformé en navire-école pour les orphelins de la marine italienne et devient un support d’apprentissage, vocation qui perdure depuis. Le gréement est simplifié et le grand salon et les cabines privées sont réunis en une seule et même salle, servant de classe, de cantine et de dortoir.
Le Belem lors de sa traversée de la Méditerranée en 12 jours pour apporter la flamme olympique d’Athènes à Marseille en vue de Paris 2024. ©Vincent Curutchet/ Caisse d’Épargne.

Cédé en 1972 aux carabiniers italiens qui restituent son gréement d’origine, puis aux chantiers navals de Venise et quasiment abandonné, il est repéré par des passionnés de marine et retrouve son nom et le pavillon français grâce notamment à la mobilisation de la Marine nationale et de Jérôme Pichard, délégué général de l’Union des Caisses d’Épargne qui le rachète et crée en 1979 la Fondation Belem Caisse d’Épargne, chargée de conserver le trois-mâts et de l’ouvrir au plus grand nombre.
Transmettre les techniques de la grande marine à voile

Après une restauration d’ampleur, le Belem, classé monument historique en 1984, reprend la mer. Il participe à de nombreux évènements, du centenaire de la statue de la Liberté en 1996, au transport de la flamme olympique jusqu’à Marseille pour les Jeux de Paris 2024. Mais il est aussi et surtout un navire-école civil. Chaque année, environ 2000 « stagiaires » embarquent pour découvrir l’art de la navigation guidée par les cartes papier et les étoiles, les techniques des matelots gabiers qui montent dans la mature pour manœuvrer les voiles et l’esprit d’équipe nécessaire au maniement d’un tel navire. « Quand un jeune professionnel de notre équipage explique à un stagiaire de 65 ans comment réaliser des gestes techniques, sur ce bateau de 130 ans, cela crée un cercle vertueux de transmission », observe le commandant Aymeric Gibet. Des jeunes aussi, repérés par des associations d’insertion, embarquent pour des stages de navigation.
Le Belem en cale sèche dans le port de Saint-Nazaire en 2023, pour le remplacement d’une partie de sa coque. ©Jérôme Bosger.

L’occasion d’observer les traces des différentes vies du Belem – les balustres et salons de l’ère britannique ou le deuxième compas qui servait sans doute pour l’enseignement à l’époque italienne – mais aussi de découvrir des métiers comme celui de maître d’équipage, ou bosco, qui fait le lien entre les matelots et le commandement, ou le maître charpentier, qui doit être capable de réparer tout ce qui peut l’être en mer. Préparation des cordages, calfatage du pont, réparation des voiles, à bord, ce sont aussi les savoir-faire liés à l’entretien traditionnel d’un voilier qui sont préservés. « Nous entretenons le gréement à l’ancienne », souligne le second capitaine Raphaël Marti, en racontant le sertissage manuel des haubans, ces câbles en acier qui maintiennent les mâts. Cet hiver, un nouveau défi se profile pour l’équipage : le démâtage complet préalable à une vaste opération de restauration. La coque, au niveau de la poupe, et la carlingue, élément essentiel de la structure du voilier, montrent des signes d’usure. Une nouvelle fois, le fameux trois-mâts va faire peau neuve, dans un chantier qui doit à la fois préserver son identité patrimoniale et garantir sa capacité à prendre la mer, là où son histoire s’est toujours écrite.
En 2025, 70 jeunes ont embarqué pour les deux premières étapes de la Tall Ships Races, reliant Le Havre, à Dunkerque, puis à Aberdeen en Écosse. © Vincent Curutchet/ Caisse d’Épargne.
La story du Belem

1896 Commandé par l’armateur Fernand Crouan, le Belem sort des Chantiers Dubigeon près de Nantes. Avec sa coque en acier, son gréement à phare carré, ses 1 200 m2 de voiles, ses vergues volantes, il est conçu pour être rapide et robuste et transporter rapidement des marchandises précieuses depuis le Brésil, la Guyane ou les Antilles, avec un équipage réduit à seulement 13 hommes. Dès son lancement, son élégance est remarquée par son armateur qui lui attribue le surnom prémonitoire de « yacht ».

1914 Alors que d’autres grands voiliers de commerce du XIXe siècle sont abandonnés, le Belem est racheté par le duc de Westminster. Il passe sous pavillon anglais et se mue en yacht de plaisance, première de nombreuses transformations et de changements d’usage qui lui ont permis de traverser les époques. Des moteurs sont installés ainsi que des salons et des cabines raffinées, desservis par un escalier à double révolution, en acajou de Cuba. Le voilier effectue de nombreux voyages sur les rivages européens, puis autour du monde.

2024 Le trois-mâts transporte la flamme des Jeux olympiques de Paris entre Athènes et le Vieux-Port de Marseille. À bord, aux côtés des seize membres professionnels de l’équipage du Belem, quatorze jeunes de toute la France sélectionnés par des associations d’insertion. Comme eux, des centaines d’autres jeunes et des milliers de passionnés embarquent chaque année pour des stages de navigation où sont transmis les savoir-faire et techniques datant de l’âge d’or de la grande marine à voile.
